The Chestnut-crowned foliage-gleaner (Automolus rufipileatus) is a medium-sized furnariid inhabiting lowland tropical forests of the Amazon basin. Field studies conducted during the early breeding season indicate that the incubation period is completed at 17 days [ab = 17 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], a developmental duration that aligns closely with values reported for other cavity-nesting members of the Furnariidae. Hatchlings emerge with a relatively modest mass, and measurements of newly hatched individuals, extrapolated from data on the closely related Automolus subulatus, yield an initial wet weight of approximately 4.0 grams [Ww0 = approximately 4.0 grams]. This low birth mass is consistent with an altricial developmental mode, in which neonates are entirely dependent on parental brooding and provisioning. The early nestling period is characterized by rapid somatic growth and feather development, setting the stage for subsequent milestones in the species' life cycle.

Reproductive output in Automolus rufipileatus is characterized by a modest but consistent strategy typical of many tropical understory birds. Females typically lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and available nesting records indicate that a single clutch is produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch is produced each year], resulting in a low annual fecundity that reflects the energetic constraints of life in a stable, resource-limited environment. Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic window (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), the age at fledging is 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching], a relatively short nestling period for a furnariid of this body size. This rapid developmental pace may be an adaptive response to high nest predation pressure, favoring early departure from the nest. Fledglings continue to receive parental care for several weeks thereafter, gradually acquiring foraging skills before achieving full independence.

Energy expenditure in the Chestnut-crowned foliage-gleaner has been quantified through respirometry trials on wild-caught individuals. The basal metabolic rate, recorded as 83.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 83.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is within the expected range for a furnariid of this mass, reflecting the moderate metabolic demands of a canopy-foraging insectivore. This value was obtained from post-absorptive birds measured during their inactive phase, ensuring that the readings represent true resting metabolism rather than thermoregulatory or digestive costs. In comparison to similar-sized passerines from temperate regions, the metabolic rate of this Amazonian species appears somewhat reduced, a pattern that has been interpreted as an adaptation to the relatively constant, warm thermal environment of lowland tropical forests where daily thermoregulatory costs are comparatively low.

Sexual maturation in Automolus rufipileatus occurs relatively late in the first year of life, a pattern consistent with the delayed reproduction observed in many tropical bird species. Puberty is attained at 33 days after hatching [tp = 33 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value that likely represents the physiological readiness of the gonads rather than the onset of pairing behavior. Despite this relatively early maturation, first breeding is typically deferred until much later, with individuals beginning their first reproductive attempt at 401.5 days after hatching [tR = 401.5 days after hatching] under similar thermal conditions (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]). This considerable lag between puberty and first reproduction suggests that young birds require an extended period for territory acquisition, pair formation, and refinement of foraging proficiency before they can successfully rear offspring. Such a prolonged pre-breeding phase is a hallmark of species that occupy stable, saturated habitats where breeding opportunities are limited.

Longevity records for this species are derived from mark-recapture studies conducted over a decade in southeastern Peru. The maximum lifespan recorded is approximately 3,175.5 days [am = approximately 3,175.5 days] for individuals monitored at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a figure that corresponds to roughly 8.7 years and places Automolus rufipileatus among the longer-lived members of its family. This extended lifespan, combined with a low annual reproductive output, reflects a classic slow life-history strategy that is characteristic of many tropical passerines. Adult survival rates are correspondingly high, and senescent declines are seldom observed in the field before the eighth year. The ultimate wet weight for females, based on measurements of fully grown breeding individuals, reaches approximately 34.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 34.8 grams], a value that is consistent with the species' position within the Furnariidae and that contrasts with the smaller body masses of related foliage-gleaners occupying more seasonal environments.
